explanations.answer: Teachers will be judged more strictly
explanations.explanation: That's the reason James gives, and he puts himself right in it. He says, “…we who teach will be judged more strictly.” (James 3:1) Notice the "we." James isn't pointing a finger from far away. He's standing in the same line as everybody else, and I respect that.

explanations.answer: Teachers will be paid too little
explanations.explanation: Nice guess, friend, but James never says a word about pay. The reason he gives is that “…we who teach will be judged more strictly.” (James 3:1) That's a heavier thing than a small paycheck. James counts himself in with that "we," so he's not pointing at anybody from a distance.

James doesn't mention friends here at all, so nobody's group chat is going quiet in this verse. He says, “…we who teach will be judged more strictly.” (James 3:1) That's the whole reason. He also says "we," which means he counts himself in.

Says is the word. James writes, “If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man, able to control his whole body.” (James 3:2) He's talking about words, friend. And since he just said we all stumble in many ways, that's a pretty high bar. I've dropped a whole tray of cookies and then said something about it I'd like to take back.

Eats isn't the word James uses. He says the one who is never at fault in what he says is a perfect man, able to control his whole body. (James 3:2) So the test is about words, not about what's on a plate. I'll admit my own self-control around fresh cookies has failed many times, but that's a different verse.

James doesn't talk about spending here, though I know that one stings for a lot of us at the end of the month. He says, “If anyone is never at fault in what he says, he is a perfect man…” (James 3:2) The word is says. Watching what comes out of your mouth is the whole point of this passage.

Right on the money. James says, “When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal.” (James 3:3) Look how small that bit is next to the horse. One little piece in the mouth, and the whole animal goes where it's guided.

Speed isn't what James is after. He says the bit is put in the horse's mouth "…to make them obey us…" and that with it “…we can guide the whole animal.” (James 3:3) So the point is steering the whole horse with one small thing. A horse that listens is a good horse, I'd say.

James doesn't say a word about a horse's meals. He says people put bits into horses' mouths to make them obey, and then they “…can guide the whole animal.” (James 3:3) Guiding is the whole idea. A small piece in the mouth, a big animal that follows.

That's it. James says ships are so large and driven by strong winds, yet “…they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined.” (James 3:4) A huge ship, a mighty wind, and a tiny rudder is what turns it. James is lining up the same lesson again: small thing, big direction.

James doesn't put any rowers on this ship. He says these ships are driven by strong winds, and then, “…they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined.” (James 3:4) The surprise is how little the steering part is. It's the opposite of a big team doing the work.

A large sail sounds reasonable, but James doesn't mention one. He says the ships are driven by strong winds, and the thing that steers them is “…a very small rudder…” (James 3:4) Small is the key word. If James had said big, the picture wouldn't work for the tongue.

True. James says, “In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things.” (James 3:5) Same pattern as the bit and the rudder: small part, big effect. He's putting the tongue right next to those two.

It's actually true. James says, “In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things.” (James 3:5) He's putting the tongue right next to the bit and the rudder. All three are small, and all three have a big say in where things go.

Yes, a forest. James says, “Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze.” (James 3:5) One little spark, and a whole forest is in trouble. That's what a small tongue can do with a few words, kind of like one text sent at the wrong moment.

A city is a fair guess, but James picks a forest. He says, “Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze.” (James 3:5) The picture is the same either way. A tiny spark can start something huge, and he's using it to talk about the tongue.

Lighting up the sky sounds pretty, and I happen to love a bright night sky. But James has something more serious in mind. He says, “Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze.” (James 3:5) A little spark can do a lot of damage, and that's his point about the tongue.

Pollutes is the word. James says the tongue “…pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.” (James 3:6) That's a strong thing to say about something so small. James isn't joking around here, and neither am I.

James says the opposite. He says the tongue “…pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.” (James 3:6) So the word he uses is pollutes. It's a serious warning, and I think he means for us to feel it.

Humbles would be a nice job for a tongue, but it's not what James says. He says the tongue “…pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.” (James 3:6) Pollutes is the word. It's a heavy verse, so take it slow.

James says the opposite. He says all kinds of animals, birds, reptiles and creatures of the sea have been tamed by man, “…but no man can tame the tongue.” (James 3:7-8) So animals get tamed, and the tongue is the hard one. I think that's the surprise he wants us to feel.

False is right. James says animals, birds, reptiles and sea creatures are being tamed and have been tamed by man, “…but no man can tame the tongue.” (James 3:7-8) He calls it “…a restless evil, full of deadly poison.” (James 3:8) A tamed animal is one thing, but a tongue is a whole other challenge.

explanations.answer: Curse people made in God's likeness
explanations.explanation: That's what James says. “With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness.” (James 3:9) Notice who's on the receiving end of the cursing: people made in God's likeness. It's the same mouth going two different directions.

explanations.answer: Lie to people who trust us
explanations.explanation: Lying is a real problem, but it's not what James names here. He says, “With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness.” (James 3:9) The other thing the tongue does is cursing. Stick with the words on the page, friend.

Gossip is a good guess, but James picks a different word. He says, “With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness.” (James 3:9) So the other thing is cursing. And he points out who gets cursed: people made in God's likeness.

James doesn't say that. After he says blessing and cursing come out of the same mouth, he adds, “My brothers, this should not be!” (James 3:10) There's no percentage that makes it okay. I think the exclamation point tells you how strongly he feels.

False is right. James says, “Out of the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, this should not be!” (James 3:10) He doesn't give a ratio that makes it fine. Blessing and cursing from the same mouth just shouldn't be, and he says so loud and clear.

James asks it as a question that has an obvious answer: “…can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs?” (James 3:12) The answer is no. A fig tree grows figs and a grapevine grows grapes. He's showing that blessing and cursing from the same mouth is just as strange.

False is right. James asks, “…can a fig tree grow olives, or a grapevine bear figs?” (James 3:12) The answer he expects is no, since a tree doesn't grow what it isn't. And he follows it with, “Neither can a salt spring produce fresh water.” (James 3:12) I'd say that settles it, friend.
